title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 41 — Global depository receipt

content.overview: Section 41 authorises a company, after passing a special resolution in its general meeting, to issue depository receipts in a foreign country in the prescribed manner and subject to prescribed conditions.
content.study:
Section 41 authorises a company, after passing a special resolution in its general meeting, to issue depository receipts in a foreign country in the prescribed manner and subject to prescribed conditions.

Statutory test
1. Corporate issuer: the action must be undertaken by a company within the statutory framework.
2. Special resolution: the company must first pass a special resolution in its general meeting.
3. Instrument: the issue is of depository receipts.
4. Territorial element: the receipts are issued in a foreign country.
5. Prescribed framework: the issue must follow the manner and conditions prescribed under the applicable rules/regulatory framework.

Application
A company approves a foreign depository-receipt issue by an ordinary board resolution alone. Advise. Identify the special-resolution requirement, then check the prescribed conditions and any separate regulatory regimes before concluding on validity or consequences.

Boundary
Section 41 differs from section 40 because section 40 regulates public offers, recognised-stock-exchange permission and public application money, whereas section 41 concerns foreign depository receipts and requires a special resolution. Section 42 concerns private placement and is not a substitute for the specific authorisation route in section 41.

sections.heading: Detailed legal explanation
sections.body: Section 41 is short but should not be reduced to the phrase 'company may issue GDRs'. The legal test begins with the corporate approval requirement: a special resolution must be passed in the general meeting. The transaction must then comply with the prescribed manner and conditions. Other applicable securities, foreign-exchange, depository, listing and regulatory requirements may operate alongside section 41; section 41 itself should not be treated as an exhaustive code for every aspect of an international depository-receipt transaction.

sections.heading: Practical illustrations
sections.body:
A company proposes a foreign depository-receipt issue without first obtaining the required special resolution. The section 41 authorisation condition has not been satisfied.

A special resolution has been passed, but the company ignores a mandatory prescribed condition governing the issue. The resolution alone does not establish full compliance.

A company analyses section 41 together with the applicable prescribed framework rather than treating the bare section as the entire transaction code.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.
